Module 1 — The Legal Engineer’s Landscape

Elephant Scale

Why Start Here

You are about to build software whose output may be read aloud in a courtroom.

That changes the acceptance criteria. “It works” is not a criterion. “It works, nothing leaked, and I can prove both” is.

This module gives you the map: what the market has already bought and what it still cannot do, what the role is, where AI actually fits in legal work. Also, the risks.

Keep this module tight — 50 minutes. It is the only module with no lab, and a room of engineers will get restless if you lecture for ninety minutes before they touch a keyboard. The market section runs from Legal AI Adoption Is Accelerating to A Policy Is Not a Control — five slides of evidence, and together they should take nine minutes, not twenty. If the room is mostly legal-tech people already, cut the EDRM section to five minutes and bank the time for Module 6.

What the Postings Actually Say and The Title Is Gated, the Work Is Not need three minutes between them and are the one thing in this module not to cut. Take those three minutes out of the adoption slide, which is scenery by comparison: put the table up, say the three headline numbers, and move.

Legal AI Adoption Is Accelerating

Three survey reports. Three different populations. One direction.

  • Twelve months earlier, one firm in five reported no GenAI engagement at all. ILTA says that holdout population “has all but vanished.”
  • For the first time in that survey’s history, an emerging technology is the primary focus of law firm technology investment.

The holdout population is gone. Adoption is no longer the question anyone is asking.

A minute, no more. This is the claim; the next slide is the evidence and the slide after it is the teaching point. If the room is legal-tech people who already know all this, say the two bullets and go straight to the verbs.

Read the population and the fieldwork date, not just the number.

  • ILTA product-level shares (Harvey, CoCounsel, Claude, Kira, Lito, “Copilot at 76%”) — these circulate in vendor blog posts; the free executive summary does not publish them.

Read the Verbs, Not the Numbers

Three reports, three different questions. The gap between 94% and 41% is mostly definitional.

  • Engaged with is not deployed. Using is not governed.
    • ILTA counts firms engaged with GenAI — evaluating it counts
    • Wolters Kluwer counts individuals who have touched a tool
    • Thomson Reuters counts organizations that say they are already using it
  • “2026” is a report title, not a field date. Two of these three were fielded in 2025.
  • A number without its population and its date is not a finding.

The adoption argument is over. Nobody has to sell AI to a law firm any more — what is left is the hard part.

Two minutes, and this is the half of the market argument to keep if you are running short. Say the definitional point out loud if anyone in the room is a researcher — pointing out the gap is worth more than the numbers are.

Fieldwork, for the record: Wolters Kluwer’s survey was fielded 8–25 August 2025 and Thomson Reuters’ in October–November 2025. Only ILTA’s is 2026 fieldwork. Adoption has moved since — the direction is the claim, not the decimal.

The Missing Piece Is Engineering

A firm can license every product in ILTA’s top twenty and still have none of the following.

What the licence does not include The 2026 evidence
Integration — find the paths AI already arrived through Among firms that enabled Copilot / Teams Premium features, Copilot Chat is the most commonly activated (81%) — capability appearing with no discrete deployment event (ILTA)
Evaluation — know whether it works, in numbers Only 18% of organizations collect any ROI metric for AI; 40% do not know whether theirs does (TR)
Customization — one policy per client, not one per firm Two-thirds of corporate clients say their outside firms should use AI, under 20% mandate it, and 40% of professionals have been told both to use AI and not to use it, depending on the client (TR)
  • ILTA’s own forecast, in its own words: firms “anticipate additional headcount needs across IT, innovation, security, training, knowledge management, and data science.”

Buying the software settles the procurement question and opens the engineering one. The engineering one is the only one a court will ask you about.

The whole argument is one move: every statistic on it is a post-purchase problem. The software was already bought. These are the things that were still missing the next morning, and each one is a line item in somebody’s budget.

Work the rows against the room. Ask who has been handed a Copilot tenant they did not provision — in a firm audience, hands go up, and that is the integration row proving itself.

The evaluation row is the setup for Module 6: 18% collecting any metric means the overwhelming majority of legal AI in production right now is unmeasured. An unmeasured review is not defensible, whoever built the tool.

If you have an engineering-only room, cut this slide to ninety seconds and keep only the evaluation row — the next slide is the other one worth keeping. Engineers do not need convincing that a licence is not a system; they need the two specific gaps this course closes.

A Policy Is Not a Control

Two of those gaps are the same gap seen from both ends — and they are the pair that bites first.

What the licence does not include The 2026 evidence
Security — a control, not a sentence in a policy GenAI entered ILTA’s tracked security-challenge list for the first time and took second place, above malware and compliance. “No confidential/sensitive info” is written policy at 29% of firms under 50 lawyers and 53% of firms over 700
Deployment — make the sanctioned path faster than the unsanctioned one 34% of law firm professionals use AI tools their firm has not authorized; 50% say their firm’s AI strategy is invisible in day-to-day work (TR)
  • “No confidential or sensitive information” is a sentence. A sentence cannot tell you where a document went.
  • And when the sanctioned path is slower than the unsanctioned one, a third of the firm has already left it — carrying client documents.
  • Both rows are your work: the control that enforces the sentence, and the sanctioned path fast enough that nobody routes around it.

You cannot write a prohibition and call it a boundary.

Slow down here. This is the row pair that makes the course’s first claim — nothing left the building — a technical problem rather than a compliance one.

A policy is a sentence, and 29% of small firms have exactly that one sentence. Plant it here and harvest it in Module 5 and again in Lab 12, where the lesson is stated as capability is not configuration — a guard that exists but is running in observe-only mode fails the question that matters.

The 34% figure is the one that lands with engineers, because they are usually part of it. Ask the room what they personally pasted into a chatbot last month. The honest answer in a firm audience is “something I should not have,” and that is the deployment row proving itself: people do not route around a control because they are careless, they route around it because it is slower than the alternative.

Sources:

  • ILTA 2026 Technology Survey, Executive Summary (full citation on Three Reports, Three Populations). The security-challenge second place and the policy table (Q3.18, broken out by firm size) are both in the free summary. ILTA’s full named concerns are GenAI-powered social engineering first, then detecting anomalous GenAI behavior, preventing GenAI agent abuse, third-party GenAI security risk, prompt injection and data/model poisoning — which is, almost line for line, the Deep Dive’s agentic-security module.
  • Thomson Reuters Institute, Future of Professionals 2026 — Legal — 736 law firm professionals across 46 countries (421 in the U.S.) plus 203 in-house, fielded March–April 2026. Verbatim: “some 34% of law firm professionals say they are currently using AI tools their firm has not authorized.” Half say their firm’s AI strategy is invisible in day-to-day work; 41% say the right tools are not yet in place. https://www.thomsonreuters.com/en/institute/future-of-professionals-2026/report-legal

What Is a “Legal Engineer”?

The person who sits between the people who know the law and the systems that process the documents.

  • Not a lawyer who learned Python
  • Not a developer who read a blog post about eDiscovery
  • Someone who can take a legal requirement — “produce every responsive, non-privileged document, and be able to defend how you found them” — and turn it into a pipeline, a metric, and an audit trail

A legal engineer’s job is to make a legal obligation executable, and then provable.

The title varies by employer: legal engineer, AI legal engineer, eDiscovery engineer, legal solutions architect, litigation support engineer, forensic technologist. Same job. Say that, so nobody disqualifies themselves over a job title.

Why This Role Is Being Hired Right Now

Three things collided:

  • Volume — matters now routinely involve millions of documents; manual review stopped being affordable years ago
  • Capability — foundation models made reading, classifying, and summarizing documents a configuration task instead of an 18-month ML project
  • Constraint — the one thing you cannot do with a legal document is send it to a stranger, and courts have started saying so in writing

The scarce skill is not “can use an LLM.” It is “can use an LLM on material that is not allowed to leave.”

Volume creates the demand. Capability makes it possible. The constraint is why they need you and not an API key.

This slide is the argument; the two market slides were the evidence for it. If anyone asked “says who?” during the adoption slide, this is where it pays off — the ILTA headcount forecast (IT, innovation, security, training, knowledge management, data science) is the industry naming this role without naming it.

The third bullet is the moat: anybody can wire a chatbot to a cloud API in an afternoon. Doing it where the data cannot leave, and producing the evidence that it did not, is a real engineering discipline.

Three caveats that must travel with these two slides:

  1. Nine postings is a sample, not a market. It establishes the title split and the platform-naming pattern, both unambiguous. It does not size demand. Do not say “the market requires” — say “these nine postings say.”
  2. Four of the nine could not be read from the employer’s own page (Dentons returns 403; Thomson Reuters and Relativity use JavaScript-rendered Workday pages). Those rows come from dated mirrors. Verify before quoting a number in marketing copy.
  3. The window moves weekly. One Gibson Dunn posting was pulled eleven days before its own published close date. Re-read the research file before teaching, and say the compile date out loud.

The Title Is Gated, the Work Is Not

  • Four of the six employers gate the role titled Legal AI Engineer behind a J.D. This course cannot satisfy that, and no course can.
  • The roles that want what you are about to build are titled something else — and the best-paid role in the set is one of them.
  • Dentons posted both, same city, same month. Legal AI Engineer wants a lawyer and publishes no salary. AI Automation Engineer wants an engineer, names RAG and ethical walls, requires no J.D., and pays $99.5k–$125k.
  • One posting in nine asks by name for what Modules 4 and 6 do — Thomson Reuters, Senior Legal AI Engineer: “measuring hallucination risk and citation quality.” It is also the only one of the nine that will take a J.D. or equivalent depth in practice.
  • What five of the six ask for and this course does not teach: the commercial platforms by name (Harvey, Copilot Studio, Azure AI Foundry, Relativity aiR, CoCounsel) and adoption — demos, onboarding, training lawyers. Know that walking in.

Read the requirements, never the headline — and when you apply, apply to the engineer-titled role.

Ninety seconds, and do not skip it. This is the slide that answers the question every paying student is already holding: will anyone hire me after this? The honest answer is yes, under a different title than the one on the brochure.

Say the J.D. line plainly and early. Someone in the room has already searched Legal AI Engineer, found a J.D. requirement, and is quietly wondering whether they are in the wrong course. They are not — they are reading the wrong half of the market. If you let them work that out on their own at the end of the course, you have lost them.

Work the Dentons pair out loud; it is the whole finding compressed into one firm. Then land the last bullet without flinching. We do not teach the platforms and we do not teach adoption. Students who hear that from you on Day 1 trust the rest of the course; students who discover it from a job posting in March do not. Point them at the handout for the platform-by-platform picture.

Who You Work For

Employer What they need from you
Legal-tech product company Ship AI features clients’ security reviews won’t kill
Law firm (litigation support / innovation) Build internal tools; keep privilege intact
Corporate legal department Reduce outside-counsel spend; govern AI use
Service provider / vendor Process at volume, defensibly, under a contract
Government / regulator / investigator Work regulated records inside a boundary (CJIS, FedRAMP)
Yourself Small firms and solos cannot afford the incumbents

The last row is underrated and worth thirty seconds. The cost floor on eDiscovery has collapsed — a capable engineer with open-source tooling and a local model can now serve small firms that were priced out entirely. That is FreeEed’s whole market thesis.

The Five Places AI Earns Its Keep

  • eDiscovery — find the responsive documents in a mountain of them

  • Document review — classify at scale: responsive, privileged, hot

  • Contracts — extract clauses, compare to a playbook, flag deviations

  • Legal research — find authority, summarize, check it (the part people skip)

  • Investigations — who knew what, when, and who did they tell

  • Underneath all five: retrieve the right text, then reason over it.

    • Modules 3 and 4 are the spine of the course

Five markets, one primitive. Build the primitive well and you can serve any of them.

Ask the room which of the five they are being paid to work on. Use the answer to decide how much of the Deep Dive material to preview. Contracts people need the extraction and agentic content; eDiscovery people need defensibility.

The EDRM, In Plain Terms

The Electronic Discovery Reference Model — the industry’s standard picture of a matter. Nine stages. You will hear it constantly, so here it is once:

Information    Identification   Preservation   Collection
Governance  ->       |        ->      |      ->     |
                     v               v              v
                 Processing   ->   Review   ->   Analysis
                     |                              |
                     v                              v
                 Production  ->  Presentation  (to the other side / the court)
  • Where your code lives: Processing, Review, Analysis, Production
  • Where your code must not break things: Preservation and Collection — that is forensic territory, where altering a byte is a sanctionable event
  • Where the money is: Review. It was always Review. Review is ~70% of the cost of a matter, and it is the part AI actually changes

Do not teach the EDRM as a framework to memorize. Teach it as a map of where your pipeline plugs in and where you must keep your hands off. The Preservation/Collection warning is the one that matters: an engineer who “normalizes” collected evidence in place has destroyed it. That is why FreeEed treats “no outbound calls and no mutation during processing” as a hard rule.

The Vocabulary That Will Cost You If You Fake It

  • Custodian — the person a document came from. Every document carries one. Your schema needs it on day one, not day thirty.
  • Responsive — relevant to the request in this matter. Not a property of the document; a property of the document and the request.
  • Privileged — protected from production (attorney-client, work product). Producing one by accident is the nightmare scenario.
  • Hot / smoking gun — the document the case turns on. Rare, high-value, and the thing everybody actually wants your tool to find.
  • Load file — the plain-text file (.dat, .opt) that carries metadata and page mappings between platforms. 1990s technology. Still how the industry moves data.
  • Bates number — the per-page identifier stamped on produced documents. The citation format of litigation.
  • Production — handing documents to the other side, in an agreed format, with an agreed manifest.

Responsiveness is relative to a request. Privilege is relative to a relationship. Neither is a document attribute — both are a judgment your system records.

That takeaway is the single most important sentence in the module for a software engineer. Developers model “responsive” as a boolean column on the document table, and then the second request arrives and the data model is wrong. Coding decisions belong to (document, matter, request), and they belong to a reviewer, with a timestamp and a reason.

Build vs. Buy

Buy when:

  • The workflow is commodity and the incumbent is good at it (hosted review platforms are)
  • You need a vendor to stand behind the output in court
  • You have no engineering capacity to own a pipeline

Build when:

  • The data cannot leave your building — this is the big one

  • Per-GB pricing on a large matter exceeds a year of engineering

  • You need a workflow nobody sells, or integration with systems nobody supports

  • You need to pin the model and reproduce a review a year later (you cannot pin somebody else’s hosted model — see Module 6)

  • Most real answers are both: buy the review platform, build the private AI layer.

“Buy” and “build” is a false binary. The real question is: which part of this is the part that has to be yours? Usually it is the part that touches the data.

Push back on anyone who says “we’d never build.” They already did — the integration glue, the load-file munger, the dedupe script. The question is whether they do it deliberately.

The model-pinning argument in the fourth build bullet is the one legal buyers have not yet internalized, and it is a durable differentiator for anything you build locally. Plant it here; harvest it in Module 6.

Risk 1 — Confidentiality and Privilege

The question: where did the document go?

  • Every document in a matter is somebody’s confidential material, and some of it is privileged
  • The moment it is sent to a third-party AI endpoint, that endpoint is in scope — of the protective order, of the client’s confidentiality obligations, of CJIS or HIPAA or whatever regime applies
  • “We have an enterprise agreement and they don’t train on our data” is a contractual answer. It is not a physical answer. Module 5 is about the difference.

You cannot un-send a document. There is no incident response for disclosure.

This is the risk engineers underrate, because in ordinary software a data-handling mistake is remediable: rotate the key, notify, patch. Privilege is not remediable. The protection either held or it didn’t, and if it didn’t, the material may be fair game. Say that plainly.

Risk 2 — Defensibility

The question: can you prove what the system did?

  • A review is not judged on whether it was right. Nobody can know that — the whole point is that no human read all the documents

  • It is judged on whether the process was reasonable and documented

  • Which means your system’s real output is not the classification. It is the record: what model, what prompt, what retrieved text, what measured recall, who approved it

  • Three things make a process defensible:

    • Measured — you have numbers (recall, elusion, precision), from a blind sample
    • Transparent — you can say why this document was coded this way
    • Reproducible — someone can re-run it and get the same determinations

In litigation, an unmeasured correct answer is worth less than a measured imperfect one.

That takeaway reliably produces an argument, which is good — have it. The engineer’s instinct is “optimize accuracy.” The legal reality is “demonstrate reasonableness.” A 78% recall review with a documented, validated methodology is defensible. A review that is probably 95% but was never sampled is not, because you have nothing to say when asked how you know.

Don’t resolve the tension here — just name it.

The Two Risks Are Why This Course Exists

The risk The claim you must be able to make Where we build it
1 Confidentiality / privilege “Nothing left the building, and here is the attestation.” Module 5, Lab 05
2 Defensibility “Here is exactly what it did, and you can re-run it.” Module 6, Lab 06

Everything else — ingestion, search, RAG, deployment — is in service of those two sentences.

Put this slide back up at the start of Day 2. It is the course’s spine, and it is what students should be able to recite a month later even if they forget every API.

Our Reference System: FreeEed

  • Open-source (Apache-2.0) eDiscovery: process, search, review, and question documents
  • Tika + Lucene/Solr + local LLM; 1,400+ file types, PST, OCR, imaging, transcription
  • Design rules that happen to be this course’s syllabus:
    • no outbound network calls during processing — forensic soundness
    • AI is local-first — nothing leaves the machine, and it can be proven

We use it as the reference architecture because it is a real product with real constraints, not because you have to adopt it.

Be straight about the commercial relationship: the instructor builds FreeEed. Say it, then move on. The reason it belongs in the course is that it is an existing production system whose design records you can read — and the labs mirror its real seams, so students are learning a shape that someone actually ships.

Discussion — Map Your Own Matter

Pair up. Ten minutes. Then we take four answers.

  1. Pick a real system you work on (or want to).
  2. Where does it sit on the EDRM?
  3. Draw where the documents go — every hop, including the AI call and the logs.
  4. Circle every hop that leaves your building.
  5. For one circled hop, answer: “Could I prove it didn’t?”

No lab for this module — step 5 is the lab, and it runs for the rest of the course.

This is the module’s only hands-on element and it is worth the time. Make them draw the logs hop — that is where people discover their prompts are being shipped to a SaaS observability vendor along with the document text. That realization is the best possible setup for Module 5, and it happens in the room rather than on a slide.

Collect two or three diagrams on the whiteboard and leave them up.

Module 1 — What You Should Leave With

  • The market: adoption is settled, implementation is not — the gap is where the role lives
  • The role: make a legal obligation executable, then provable
  • The titles: Legal AI Engineer is often J.D.-gated — apply to the engineer-titled role
  • The map: EDRM — your code lives in Processing, Review, Analysis, Production
  • The vocabulary: custodian, responsive, privileged, load file, Bates, production
  • The data-model lesson: coding decisions belong to (document, matter, request, reviewer)
  • The two risks: where did it go? and can you prove what it did?

Next: the data itself. It is worse than you think, and that is the job.
